nameStory: This beetle gets its "yellow-horned" name from its distinctive yellowish antennae that stand out like golden horns against its darker body. The "flower longhorn" part comes from its habit of visiting flowers for nectar and pollen, while sporting the characteristically long antennae that give all longhorn beetles their name.
description: The Yellow-horned Flower Longhorn Beetle is a slender, medium-sized beetle that you'll often find crawling around on flowers during summer days. Like other longhorn beetles, it has impressively long antennae that can be as long as or longer than its body. These beetles are typically dark-colored with yellowish antennae and legs, and they move with a somewhat clumsy, deliberate gait as they search for pollen and nectar. Adults usually measure about half an inch to three-quarters of an inch long.

idTips.label: Yellow antennae
idTips.description: Look for distinctly yellowish or pale antennae that contrast with the darker body - they feel smooth and segmented if you gently touch them

idTips.label: Flower behavior
idTips.description: Often found crawling on flower heads, especially white flowers, moving slowly and deliberately as they feed on pollen

idTips.label: Body shape
idTips.description: Slender, elongated beetle with a somewhat flattened appearance and smooth, hard wing covers that feel glossy to the touch

idTips.label: Leg color
idTips.description: Legs are typically yellowish or pale, matching the antennae color, and move in a slow, methodical walking pattern

idTips.label: Size and proportions
idTips.description: Medium-sized beetle with antennae nearly as long as the entire body, giving it a distinctly leggy appearance

habitat: Look for Yellow-horned Flower Longhorn Beetles in forest edges, woodland clearings, and gardens where flowering shrubs and wildflowers bloom. They're particularly fond of areas with native flowering plants like wild hydrangea and lizard's tail, but will visit cultivated gardens with abundant blooms. You'll find them from sea level to moderate elevations throughout New England's mixed hardwood and coniferous forests.

seasonality.spring: Adults begin emerging in late spring but are not commonly seen yet. Look for early flowers where they might start appearing in warmer areas.
seasonality.summer: Peak activity time! Adults are actively feeding on flowers, mating, and laying eggs. This is when you're most likely to spot them crawling on flower heads during warm, sunny days.
seasonality.fall: Adult activity winds down as temperatures drop. Late-season flowers may still attract a few individuals, but they become increasingly rare to find.
seasonality.winter: No adult activity. The beetles are in their larval stage, developing inside dead or dying wood where they'll spend the cold months.

funFact: Female Yellow-horned Flower Longhorn Beetles have been observed acting like tiny gourmets - they don't just visit flowers randomly, but actually consume pollen from specific plants while mating, essentially having a romantic dinner date that doubles as egg-preparation nutrition!
confusionNotes: Most easily confused with its relative, the Slender Flower Longhorn Beetle, but the yellow antennae are the dead giveaway - remember "yellow horns, yellow-horned beetle" as your memory trick. Other longhorn beetles visiting flowers typically have darker or differently colored antennae.
contextualKnowledge: Don't confuse these beneficial flower-visiting longhorns with destructive wood-boring longhorn beetles that damage trees and structures. Yellow-horned Flower Longhorns are actually helpful pollinators as adults, though their larvae do develop in dead wood, making them important decomposers in forest ecosystems.
compareHints: The Yellow-horned Flower Longhorn differs from its close relative the Slender Flower Longhorn primarily in antenna color - the Slender species typically has darker antennae. Both species visit flowers and have similar body shapes, but the distinctive pale yellow antennae make the Yellow-horned species relatively easy to distinguish. The Yellow-horned also tends to be slightly more robust in build compared to its more delicate-looking cousin.

relatedSpecies.distinction: The Slender Flower Longhorn is distinguished from its close relative, the Yellow-horned Flower Longhorn Beetle, primarily by antenna color - this species has dark antennae while the Yellow-horned has bright yellowish antennae.
